prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Context: National Airspace System (NAS); air traffic management (ATM) system; actors: controllers, airspace users, Federal Aviation Administration (FAA); stakeholders and automation systems receive no direct communication of current tactical controller actions.
Current ATM: The ATM system predicts each flight’s trajectory from its approved flight plan and scheduled or controlled departure time. Strategic management implements changes through flight plan changes and is conservative to avoid unnecessary delays. Once an aircraft moves, controllers tactically manage it using “open trajectory” vectors, altitude changes, and speed clearances to implement traffic management restrictions, separate conflicting aircraft, and address NAS constraints. Tactical problems include weather avoidance and compliance with new Traffic Flow Management (TFM) restrictions. Uncommunicated controller actions and gaps in trajectory prediction data/models impede prediction of constraint effects.
Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times intended to satisfy a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) at a NAS constraint. They use the airspace user’s estimated time en route without knowledge of controller actions addressing other constraints. Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) similarly assumes estimated times of arrival (ETAs) at constraints are correct. Disruptions and local traffic management decisions can cause unexpected delays; effects on individual flights remain unknown until experienced, and multiple disruptions reduce demand-prediction accuracy at NAS resources.
Future concept: Management by Trajectory (MBT) is future ATM in which FAA and airspace users negotiate four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all flights. Negotiated 4DTs communicate the traffic management plan. Trajectories must respect airspace user goals while complying with NAS constraints; the concept considers both FAA and airspace user objectives and accommodates different airspace user types and trajectory characteristics.

Document units:
U0013: As a result, the baseline concept accommodates a broad and expanding spectrum of current and anticipated airspace operations, from traditional commercial aviation to emerging users such as Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, and on-demand air transportation vehicles.
U0014: Pilots and air traffic controllers use automation to keep the aircraft on its assigned trajectory, which includes complying with temporal or speed constraints.
U0015: Equipped aircraft have substantial responsibility for complying with the assigned trajectory without controller intervention.
U0016: Assigned trajectories are constructed to respect all of the known constraints from the aircraft’s current location to its destination, making the flight’s entire trajectory much more predictable than it is today.
U0017: Where uncertainty or disruptions occur, resolutions are, to the extent possible, handled through trajectory modifications as far in advance as possible.
U0018: Future improvements in automation (ground-based and aircraft) and data communications (air-ground and among stakeholders on the ground) make the MBT concept possible.
U0019: MBT eliminates most local, reactive control actions being applied to aircraft, which cannot be predicted in advance and which have impacts on the downstream trajectory that cannot be known until they happen.
U0020: MBT does this by inserting the impact of all NAS constraints into the assigned trajectory in the form of trajectory constraints.
U0021: Where uncertainty remains, necessary adjustments to the trajectory constraints are made proactively, maximizing trajectory predictability and delivering associated benefits. 1 In this way, MBT is similar to Trajectory Based Operations concepts that employ a 4D contract.
U0022: The appendix “Comparison with ICAO TBO Concept” compares MBT with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO concept.
U0023: In the past decade, the term Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) has been used widely.
U0024: The term TBO has come to be used in two distinct ways.
U0025: One meaning of TBO is as a high-level vision for the future of the NAS in which 4DTs are the core of air traffic control and air traffic management.
U0026: The second meaning of TBO is an evolving set of specific endeavors intended to advance the NAS toward the future vision.
